DILG Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA comer Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City http: Ilwww.dilg.com.ph DILG OPINION No. 10 s. 2023 MAR 23 nn HON. WALLACE R. SINACA Mayor, Municipality of Malimono Surigao del Norte Dear Mayor Sinaca: This refers to your letter dated February 20, 2023 requesting for this Department's legal opinion concerning the internal rules of the Sangguniang Bayan members of Malimono, specifically Sections III to II I, Rule XIX thereof. As premised, the herein request for a legal opinion stems from the clamor of several Sangguniang Bayan (SB) members concerning their internal rules, specifically Sections III to 115, Rule XIX thereof, which govern their sessions, thus: "Rule XIX Supplementary Rules Xxx Section 111. The presence of a Police Officer outside of the session hall shall be considered to assist the Presiding Officer in ensuring peace and order during the conduct of sessions. Section 112. Only media personalities, internal and external guests and/or observers with prior authorized by the majority of the members, there being a quorum, shall be allowed to stay inside the session hall during the conduct of session due its limited space. Section 113. Media coverage, video and/or audio recording of the session proceedings is upon two-thirds (2/3) vote of the members in attendance. Section 114. Cellphones and all other digital/electronic device are strictly prohibited inside the session hall. When brought inside the session hall, such shall be turned off and handed over to a legislative staff assigned for the purpose. Section 115. Bags brought inside the session hall shall be presented for inspection by a legislative staff assigned for the purpose." At the outset, it is to be noted that while the Local Government Code of 1991 (Republic Act No. 7160, hereinafter referred to as the Code) grants local sanggunians the prerogative to promulgate their own internal rules of procedure on matters pertaining to parliamentary rules and conduct of decorum during their session, the same should not contravene the Code or any existing laws, much less the Constitution. With that said, attention is now respectfully directed to pertinent provisions of the Code, thus: Matino, Mahusay at Maasahan" Trunkline No.: 8876-34-54

"Section 52. Sessions. — Xxx (c) All sanggunian sessions shall be open to the public unless a closed-door session is ordered by an affirmative vote of a majority of the members present, there being a quorum, in the public interest or for reasons of security, decency, or morality. No two (2) sessions, regular or special, may be held in a single day. " As could be clearly gleaned from the above-cited provision, the general rule is that sanggunian sessions should be open to the public. Stated differently, sanggunian sessions should not be restricted to certain individuals, i.e., media personalities and internal and external guests. The Code, however, holds utmost importance and high regard for the public interest. Likewise, the Code is not oblivious to the significance of holding sessions in a secure, decent, and moral atmosphere. It is solely for these reasons that the law permits the sanggunian to conduct its session behind closed doors. Accordingly, the conduct of closed-door sessions for any reason other than those that are explicitly provided by the Code is an utter contravention of the Code. It is respectfully opined that Section 112 of the internal rule of the herein concerned sanggunian appears to run counter to the clear provision of the Code. To our view, the prior authorization from the majority of the SB members is uncalled for. Similarly, Section 113 thereof, insofar as it requires a two-thirds (2/3) vote of the SB members present during such a session for media coverage, appears to be untenable. Such a requirement undermines the transparency and accountability of sanggunian and, more importantly, the freedom of the public to information. No less than the 1987 Constitution, specifically Section 7, Article Ill thereof, provides that "The right of the people to information on matters of public concem shall be recognized. Access to official records, and to documents and papers pertaining to official acts, transactions, or decisions, as well as to government research data used as basis for policy development, shall be afforded the citizen, subject to such limitations as may be provided by law. " Corollarily, Executive Order (EO) No. 2 series of 2016 was issued to operationalize the constitutional dictum on public disclosure of state transactions involving public interests, and the right of people to information on matters of public concern. It also encourages local governments to observe and, accordingly, be guided by the said EO. In 2018, this Department, together with the Presidential Communications Operations Office, jointly issued Memorandum Circular No. 2018-011 reiterating pertinent provisions of the aforesaid EO. As to Section 111 of the internal rules in question, we are of the view that if there is a clear and eminent danger in the conduct of the session, the presence of a police officer outside the session hall may be allowed. Going now to Section 113, it is this Department's view that the media coverage, video, 1 PCOO-DILG Joint Memorandum Circular No. 2018-01. dated October 9, 2018 (Reiteration of Execution Order No. 2, S. 2016, "Operationalizing the People's Right to Information and the State Policies of Full Public Disclosure and Transparency in the Public Service). and/or recording of the session proceeding should not be contingent upon the two- thirds (2/3) vote of the SB members present during such a session, but of the elements as specified under Section 52 (c) of the Code. With regard to Sections 114 and 115, we also find the provisions therein to be unwarranted. We concur with your observations that the restriction of electronic gadgets or equipment is an apparent deprivation of property without due process of law. As you aptly pointed out, Section I of the Bill of Rights of the 1987 Constitution provides that "No person shall be deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process of law." Similarly, the presentation of bags for inspection by a legislative staff appears to be an encroachment on the privacy of the SB members. As you pointed out, Section 2 of the Bill of Rights provides that "The right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects against unreasonable searches and seizures of whatever nature and for any purpose shall be inviolable. " On a final note, it is to be emphasized that the sanggunian's internal rules of procedure do not have the imprints of permanence and obligatoriness during their effectivity since they do not have the force of law but are merely in the nature of by-laws designed for the orderly and convenient conduct of proceedings. They may even be waived or disregarded with the concurrence of the majority of the members adopting them.2 This opinion is being rendered without prejudice to any contrary opinion of competent authorities and the courts. We hope to have guided you accordingly. Thank you. Very truly yours, y the Aut ority of the Secret Und ous cc ANV OR R.
